# fael-sweep — every open issue gets a chunk or a question

You read the open issues, judge them against the code, and leave each one on the board in a
state the owner can act on in one step: a chunk to approve, or a question to answer. You read
code and write chunks — that is all. The owner approves and closes; the agents the owner sends
fix, each with `fael-debug`.

**An issue with a chunk linked is triaged.** That link (`chunk add --issue`) is the only record
that this skill saw it — so every issue you judge gets one, including the ones that cannot be
fixed. A second sweep skips them.

## 1. One read

```bash
fael sweep --input
```

This repo only, one command: `issues[]` is every untriaged open issue with its body
(`title`, `text`), its shared-file `group`, and the commits naming it (`commits`,
one git log for every id — never a log per issue, never `fael find` per body).
`active_scopes[]` is the scope of every open/running/waiting chunk, `claimed[]`
the issues someone holds — together the work already in flight a new chunk must
not collide with. `drifted[]` is the drifted decisions/notes with `from`, the
file that moved most (`top_file`) and its count.

Nothing untriaged → say so in one line and go to the drifted pass (step 7).

## 2. Judge each issue against the code

**Commits first.** `issues[].commits[]` already names the fix commits (one git log
for every id: `git log --format="%H %s" --grep=<a> --grep=<b> ... HEAD`, ORed, mapped
back per id — never a log per issue). A fix commit that names the id → `drop?`
(already fixed), that commit as the evidence; don't open the code.

Per issue left: the body is in `issues[]` — open the files and symbols it names
(`fael find <id>` only when you need neighbours). Decide from what the code does
now, not from the title:

| Verdict | When |
|---|---|
| **fix** | the cause is visible in the code, or a repro is one command away |
| **ask owner** | the fix needs a choice only the owner can make (behaviour, scope, a product call) |
| **need data** | cannot reproduce; the fix waits on a log, a sample, a user report |
| **drop?** | already fixed, not a bug, outside this repo, or not worth it — say which, with evidence |

Already fixed in the code? It is still a `drop?`: the owner closes the issue, not you.

## 3. Group and order

- **One chunk** for issues with one cause, or whose fix edits the same lines — `--issue a,b`.
  The board's `group` is a hint (shared files), not the verdict: two issues on one file with
  unrelated causes stay two chunks.
- **scope** = the paths the fix will edit, from the code you read.
  It is what lets two agents run side by side; a wrong scope puts two agents on one file.
- **Parallel** = no `--after`. **Ordered** = scopes overlap, or one fix needs the other's
  output: `--after <uid>` on the later one. A scope that overlaps a chunk already in
  flight goes `--after` that chunk too — in flight means `running` or claimed
  (`claimed[]`, a live run holding it). An `open` or `waiting` chunk nobody started
  does not block: order past it, never after it.
- **size / model**: S (an hour, mechanical, one file) → `sonnet`; M (a session, cause clear
  but spread) → `sonnet` or `opus`; cause unclear or cross-module → `opus`. L → split it.

## 4. The plan table

One table:

```
#  issues          verdict    title                         scope              after  size/model
1  01M4…, 01M4…    fix        Export pages past 1000 rows   src/export.rs      —      S sonnet
2  01M4…           fix        …                             src/export.rs      #1     M opus
3  01M4…           ask owner  Cap or page the export?       —                  —      —
```

Where it goes depends on how you were started:

- **In chat** (the owner typed `/fael-sweep`): show it, ask **"Tell me what's wrong with it."**,
  apply the corrections, and write only after the owner's yes.
- **As a chunk** (you ran `fael chunk start` on a sweep chunk, e.g. from the board): nobody is
  in the chat to answer, so write it now (step 5); the table is your `chunk done`
  hand-off (step 6). Nothing you write starts before the owner approves it on the board, so
  that approval is the yes.

## 5. Write

Every brief is English and stands alone: the cause as you found it (symbol, file), what to
change, what to leave alone, how it is checked (the repro or test that fails today), the issue
ids, and "fix with /fael-debug". Add in plan order so `--after` can name a uid already printed.

**fix:**

```bash
fael chunk add "<title>" --plan inbox --brief "<brief>" --issue <ids> \
  --scope <paths> --size S|M --model <m> [--after <uid>]
```

Priority lives on the row, not the chunk: `fael add --urgent`, `fael add --urgent-before <id>`,
`fael bump --urgent|--urgent-before <id>|--not-urgent` (still true after its files changed).

**ask owner / need data / drop?** — a chunk that waits, so the question sits on the board,
one command (add + start --no-worktree + wait are one call):

```bash
fael chunk add "<title>" --plan inbox --brief "<what to do once answered>" \
  --issue <ids> [--scope <paths>] --size S|M --model <m> \
  --wait owner --ask "<question>" [--option "A" --option "B" ...]          # drop? and ask owner
fael chunk add "<title>" --plan inbox --brief "<what to do once answered>" \
  --issue <ids> [--scope <paths>] --size S|M --model <m> \
  --wait data --ask "<what is missing>" [--until YYYY-MM-DD]               # need data
```

A `drop?` verdict puts `drop?` in the title or the brief (e.g. `drop? already fixed
in <file>: <symbol>`): dropping that chunk also closes its linked issues.
A path the brief deliberately scopes out says `leave alone` on its line, so no
scope warning fires for it.

The wait text is what the owner reads on the board, so it carries the whole decision:
the question, 2–3 options each with what it costs, and **your recommendation and why** —
`drop?` recommends the drop and names the evidence. The owner answers with
`fael chunk answer <uid> "<choice>"` (back to `open`, the answer printed in its next brief) or
drops it.

Leave every chunk unapproved: approval is the owner's, and it is what lets the queue start one.

## 6. Hand back

Three lines: how many chunks to approve (parallel / ordered), how many questions waiting on the
owner, how many on data. Then `fael board` — that is where the owner acts.

Then the drifted pass (step 7). As a chunk, those lines, the table and the drifted report are
the hand-off: `fael chunk done <uid> "<lines + table + report>"` (no PR — it lands in review,
where the owner reads it and accepts).

## 7. Drifted pass — decisions and notes, one file at a time

A decision or note whose files took 10+ commits since it was written is `drifted` (`.md`
files count only for a row that names no code): the code
moved on, so the row may now restate it, contradict it, or still hold. Settle each one here.
Same rule as above: you read code and write ledger rows — never code, never a delete
(no `fael purge`).

**Input.** From the same `fael sweep --input`: `drifted[]` already carries `from`,
the file that moved most (`top_file`) and its count (`top_count`, `total`) — one
`git log` for every row, already grouped by file. (`fael doctor` [Drifted] lists the
same ids.) None → one line, stop.

A row with `from: "user"` is always **ask**: the user said it; only the user retires
it. Take it out before anything is judged.

**Who judges.** A sub-agent costs its start-up, not its reads, so spend one only on a file
with 3+ rows. Files with fewer rows you judge yourself, or pack all of them into one
sub-agent. Never one sub-agent per one-row file. A sub-agent (haiku is enough) gets only:

- its files' rows: bodies are in `drifted[]` (`fael find <id>` only for neighbours);
- what changed since each row: `git log --since=<oldest row at> -p -- <file>`, trimmed to the
  hunks that touch what the rows name; the log too long to read → the file at HEAD instead.

Never the whole ledger, never other files' rows. It returns one verdict per row:

| Verdict | When | Command |
|---|---|---|
| **close** | the code holds it now — the row restates it | `fael close <id> "now in <file>: <symbol or line>"` |
| **bump** | still true, and the code alone would not tell a new agent | `fael bump <id>` |
| **supersede** | wrong now; one passage changes | `fael add <kind> --supersedes <id> --replace "<old passage>" --with "<new>"` (no text: it keeps the row's text, title, files, key) |
| | wrong now; most of it changes | `fael add <kind> "<new text>" --title "<t>" --files <same files> [--key <same key>] --supersedes <id>` |
| **ask** | unsure — the owner decides | none |

The sub-agent judges; you run the commands. Before you do, open the place each **close** cites:
a test string, a comment or a fixture is not the code holding it — that row is a bump.

**Run per file**, the group's commands chained with `&&` in one shell call, so one failure
stops that file and the rest of the group stays for a rerun:

```bash
fael close 01M4… "now in fael/src/hook/push.rs: row_lines()" && fael bump 01M4… && \
  fael add decision --supersedes 01M4… --replace "<old passage>" --with "<new>"
```

**Report** — three lines, then the asks:

```
drifted: 14 files read · 32 rows judged
close 18 · bump 7 · supersede 3 · ask 4
ask: 01M4… (from:user) — <question in one line> · 01M4… — <what the code does vs what the row says>
```

In chat, put each ask to the owner; as a chunk, they go in the `chunk done` hand-off with the
table. `fael doctor` [Drifted] after the pass shows only the asks.

## After a sweep

- An approved chunk runs; its agent fixes with `fael-debug` and ends with `fael chunk done`.
- A chunk done while its issue is still open shows under needs you `issue-open`: the agent or
  the owner runs `fael close <id> "<why>"` once the fix holds. Then the issue leaves the board.
- A chunk the owner dropped keeps its issue triaged: the sweep will not raise it again. Close
  the issue too if it is not a bug.
